title: The Personal Tax Lifecycle: Earn, Defer, Draw
summary: An owner-manager's taxes follow a lifecycle: how income leaves the company, where savings are sheltered, and in what order money is drawn in retirement. This lesson sets out the concepts of salary versus dividend, integration, and tax-deferred versus tax-free accounts, without stating any jurisdiction's rates or rules.
body:
The tax you pay over a lifetime depends less on any single year's rate than on three recurring choices: how money leaves your company, where you keep what you save, and in what order you draw it back out.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between a fiduciary duty and a suitability standard?

A. A fiduciary must act loyally in your interest and manage conflicts. A suitability standard, in general terms, only requires that a recommendation fit your circumstances. Which applies depends on the adviser's licence, service and jurisdiction.

Q. What are the three handovers in succession?

A. Ownership, control and knowledge. A will moves ownership; control and knowledge need their own plan.

Q. Why do fees and conflicts matter as much as asset class when investing beyond real estate?

A. Because a layered fee compounds against you every year, and a conflicted recommendation may suit the adviser more than you, regardless of how good the asset class is.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer who works through companies decides every year how to pay himself. That choice has consequences that run for decades: it affects how much you can shelter in retirement accounts, whether you build entitlement to public pensions, how much tax is deferred inside the company, and how you will eventually draw an income. Most owners make it by default, whatever the accountant did last year. This week makes it deliberate.

I teach concepts here. Every rule, rate, limit and deadline differs by jurisdiction and changes over time. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it, and have a tax adviser confirm any decision.

The lifecycle in three phases

Plain English. Accumulation is the earning years, when income exceeds spending and you build wealth. Transition is the years around stepping back, when you reorganise what you own, perhaps sell a business, and decide how income will be produced. Decumulation is drawing down: living on savings, pensions and investment income.

The tax question changes in each. In accumulation the question is how to extract and save money efficiently. In transition it is how to realise value, such as a sale or a freeze, without unnecessary tax. In decumulation it is the order in which to draw from different pools so lifetime tax stays low and income stays steady.

Salary versus dividend

An owner-manager can usually take money from a company in two main ways. A salary is employment income: deductible to the company, taxed to you as earnings, and in many systems subject to payroll contributions. A dividend is a distribution of after-tax company profit to shareholders: not deductible to the company, taxed to you as investment income, often at a different rate that allows for tax the company has already paid.

The professional idea that connects them is integration: the design principle, in some tax systems, that income earned through a company and paid out as a dividend should bear roughly the same total tax as the same income earned directly. Where integration works well, the choice between salary and dividend is close on tax alone, and the decision turns on everything else. Where it does not, one route can be materially cheaper. Whether and how well a given system integrates is a jurisdiction-specific question.

The "everything else" is often decisive. In many systems, salary creates earned income that generates room to contribute to retirement accounts and builds entitlement to contributory public pensions; dividends typically do not. Salary may be required to qualify for certain benefits or to demonstrate income to a lender. Dividends avoid payroll contributions and can be timed more flexibly. Neither is right in general.

Say that out loud now.

Applied example, hypothetical. An owner takes no salary for fifteen years, only dividends, because each year's tax comparison looked slightly better. At sixty he discovers he has built little retirement account room and little contributory pension entitlement, so a larger share of his retirement income will come from taxable sources. Each annual decision was defensible; the lifetime result was not, because no one looked at the lifecycle. Day 2 takes that pattern apart.

Where savings live

Savings can sit in three broad kinds of pool. A taxable account, where income and gains are taxed as they arise or are realised. A tax-deferred account, where contributions may be deductible, growth is untaxed while inside, and withdrawals are taxed as income; many retirement plans work this way. A tax-free account, where contributions are made from after-tax money, growth is untaxed, and qualifying withdrawals are not taxed. In Canada, the registered retirement savings plan is commonly described as tax-deferred and the tax-free savings account as tax-free; their limits and rules must be checked against the current primary source.

There is a fourth pool for owner-managers: money left inside the company. Profit taxed at the corporate level and left there may defer personal tax until it is paid out. Some systems then apply special rules to passive investment income earned inside a company, which can change the arithmetic. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Applied example, hypothetical. A developer has 100,000 dollars to save this year. A tax-deferred account suits a year when his tax rate is high and he expects it to be lower in retirement. A tax-free account suits a year when his rate is low, or when he wants flexible access. Leaving it in the company suits a year when he needs the money for project equity soon. The same dollar has a different best home depending on the year.

How the best do it

The practice that distinguishes good private-client tax advice, described here without naming any firm, is the multi-year plan. Instead of minimising this year's tax, the adviser projects income, tax and account balances over ten or twenty years, including a planned sale and retirement, and asks which sequence of salaries, dividends, contributions and withdrawals produces the lowest lifetime tax and the steadiest after-tax income. A small developer can copy it with a spreadsheet and an annual meeting: one page showing the next ten years, updated each year, instead of a one-year decision made at the year-end deadline.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: optimise the lifetime, not the year. Liability: money left in an operating company is exposed to that company's creditors, so surplus may belong in a separate holding entity, subject to advice. Banking: lenders often want to see personal income, which a dividend-only history can make harder to show. Governance: record each year's compensation decision by resolution. Estate: different pools are treated differently at death, so their mix affects the estate. Exit: how you hold shares at sale can change the tax on the sale itself.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser or accountant, on compensation, contributions and withdrawal order.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is optimising each year in isolation, so a sequence of small annual wins adds up to a lifetime of lost retirement room and higher tax in decumulation. The control is a written ten-year tax projection, reviewed every year before the compensation decision.

The beginner's mistake

Asking only "which is cheaper this year, salary or dividend?" The beginner never asks what each choice builds or forgoes for later: retirement room, pension entitlement, borrowing evidence and flexibility.

Callback

In Week 22, Elias taught that tax depends on character: income versus capital, earned versus investment, and who earns it. The salary-versus-dividend choice is that idea applied to yourself every year. The same dollar of company profit changes character depending on how it leaves the company, and the character decides what it builds.

Recap

The lifecycle runs from accumulation through transition to decumulation. Salary and dividend differ in tax and in what they build; integration aims to equalise their tax. Savings live in taxable, tax-deferred, tax-free and corporate pools. Plan over ten years, not one.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: a composite case of an owner who paid himself only dividends for twenty years.
checklist: I know which lifecycle phase I am in and what tax question it raises.
I decide salary and dividend each year against a ten-year projection.
I know what salary builds that dividends do not in my jurisdiction.
I use each savings pool for the years it suits best.
I check special rules for passive income left inside a company.
I record each year's compensation decision by resolution.
A tax adviser confirms every rule and limit against the current primary source.
head: Field checklist
speak: Your lifetime tax depends on three recurring choices: how money leaves your company, where you keep what you save, and in what order you draw it out. The lifecycle runs from accumulation, through transition around a sale or stepping back, to decumulation. Salary is deductible to the company and taxed to you as earnings; a dividend comes from after-tax profit and is taxed as investment income. Integration is the design aim, in some systems, that both routes bear roughly the same total tax. Where they are close, the deciding factors are what each builds: in many systems salary creates retirement account room, pension entitlement and evidence of income for lenders, and dividends do not. Savings can sit in taxable, tax-deferred, tax-free and corporate pools, each suited to different years. All rules and rates vary by jurisdiction, so plan over ten years with a tax adviser, not one year at the deadline.
terms: Integration — the design aim, in some tax systems, that income earned through a company and paid as a dividend bears roughly the same total tax as income earned directly.
Decumulation — the phase of life in which a person draws down savings and pensions to fund spending.
Tax-deferred account — an account where tax on contributions or growth is postponed until money is withdrawn.

hostile.q: Your accountant has paid you dividends only for years because it was cheaper. Why change now?
hostile.a: Because cheaper each year is not cheaper over a lifetime. A ten-year projection shows that a salary component builds retirement room and pension entitlement that dividends do not, and helps when a lender asks for personal income. I'll set the mix each year against that projection, with my accountant confirming the rules.

title: Twenty Years of Cheapest-This-Year
summary: A composite case: an owner-manager took only dividends for two decades, left surplus to pile up inside his operating company, and never projected beyond the year-end. At sixty he had little retirement room, a trapped surplus exposed to a project claim, and a tax bill to extract it. Seven forensic steps show where it went wrong.
body:
This is a composite example. An owner made the cheapest tax choice every single year for twenty years, and at the end found that the sum of those choices was expensive, inflexible and exposed.

Recall

Q. In reverse engineering a portfolio, what is an annuity factor?

A. The multiplier that converts a level annual withdrawal over a period into the lump sum needed today at a given real return.

Q. In the Week 93 composite, what was the point of no return for the family company?

A. The founder's death without a signed shareholders' agreement, because after it every term moved money between siblings who no longer shared interests.

Q. What is correlation, and why does it matter in a portfolio?

A. The degree to which assets move together. Assets that fall together in the same conditions do not protect one another.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because no law was broken here and no adviser was dishonest. Each year's return was prepared correctly. The failure is one of planning horizon, and it is common among successful owner-managers precisely because each annual decision is defensible. This is a composite example drawn from recurring patterns; every number is hypothetical, and no jurisdiction's rules are being stated.

1. Timeline

Year 1: an owner incorporates a small development and property company. His accountant compares salary and dividend at year-end and finds dividends slightly cheaper once payroll contributions are counted. He takes dividends only. Years 2 to 10: the same comparison, the same answer. The company does well, and he leaves surplus profit inside it, because taking it out would trigger personal tax. Years 11 to 18: the surplus grows to a hypothetical 3,000,000 dollars of cash and investments, held in the same company that builds projects and signs guarantees. Year 19: a project the company built has a defect claim, and the claimant pursues the company, whose largest asset is now the surplus. Year 20: the owner, now sixty, wants to retire. He has built little retirement account room and little contributory pension entitlement, his surplus is tied up in the claim, and getting the rest out will be taxed as he draws it.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Making the compensation choice every year on that year's tax alone. Leaving surplus in the operating company rather than moving it, subject to advice, into a separate entity away from project risk. And never projecting the retirement phase, so nobody asked how the surplus would eventually come out.

3. Assumptions

The owner assumed that lower tax this year meant lower tax overall. He assumed money in his company was as safe as money in his own name. He assumed retirement would sort itself out, because the company would always be worth enough. And he assumed his accountant was planning, when the accountant had been engaged to prepare returns.

4. Incentives

The accountant was paid to file accurate returns and to minimise the year's tax, and did both. Nobody was paid to think twenty years ahead. The owner felt each year's saving immediately and the long-term cost not at all, which is the classic shape of a decision that goes wrong slowly. The tax system itself, by deferring tax on retained profit, rewarded leaving money where it was.

Say that out loud now.

5. Warning signs ignored

First, a lender asked for proof of personal income when he applied for a mortgage in year 9, and dividend history made it harder; he treated it as an inconvenience. Second, the company's lawyer remarked in year 12 that the surplus was sitting in the entity that carried construction risk. Third, his accountant's engagement letter said "compliance services", which nobody read as "no planning". Fourth, he had no written retirement income figure at any point. Each sign pointed to the same gap: nobody owned the lifetime view.

6. Point of no return

There were two. For the surplus, it was the defect claim: once a claim exists, moving money out of the company may be attacked as defeating a creditor, which is the voidable transfer problem from Week 89. Before the claim, a reorganisation on advice could have been legitimate; after it, the same step looks like flight. For retirement room, the loss built year by year; there was no single moment, which is why nobody noticed.

7. Root cause

The root cause was a one-year planning horizon applied to a forty-year problem. Cole states it as an audit finding: the owner had a tax return for every year and a tax plan for none. Every decision was optimised locally, and nobody was responsible for the whole sequence.

Cole's reconstruction

Cole's method in a case like this is to rebuild the twenty years as a table, one row a year, with four columns: what was taken out and how, what was left in the company, what retirement room was created, and what the year's comparison claimed to save. Done for this composite, the "saving" column shows a modest figure each year, say a few thousand dollars in the illustrative arithmetic, and the "room created" column shows almost nothing. Added up, the savings are a visible but small total. The room forgone, compounded at an assumed real return for the years until retirement, is a much larger number, because sheltered growth on money that was never contributed is growth that was never sheltered.

The point of the table is not the precise figures, which depend entirely on rules and rates that vary by jurisdiction. It is that the cost and the saving sit in different columns, and the annual decision only ever looked at one of them. An audit of your own plan should rebuild the same four columns for the last five years, and ask an adviser what the next ten would look like if nothing changed.

What would have stopped it

The same owner, with a ten-year projection from year 1. In some years a salary large enough to build retirement room and pension entitlement, with dividends on top. Surplus moved periodically, after advice and while no claim existed, into a holding company away from project risk, or into personal savings pools. A written retirement income target, reviewed each year. And an engagement letter that bought planning as well as compliance. None of it required unusual structures. It required someone to look forward.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser, on compensation mix and extraction; corporate lawyer, on moving surplus out of an operating company and the creditor-protection rules that apply.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a horizon mismatch: annual decisions for a lifetime problem, so the costs arrive at retirement when they can no longer be fixed. The control is a ten-year tax and retirement projection, owned by a named adviser under an engagement that includes planning, reviewed before every year-end decision.

The beginner's mistake

Leaving surplus in the operating company because extracting it costs tax this year. The beginner sees the tax and not the exposure: money that sits in the entity carrying construction risk is money a claimant can reach.

Callback

In Week 89, Omar and Tessa taught that asset protection depends on timing: a transfer made before any claim, for good reason, stands far better than one made after. This case failed on exactly that point. Moving the surplus in year 12, when the lawyer raised it, was planning; trying in year 19, after the claim, would have looked like a fraudulent transfer.

Recap

A composite owner took the cheapest tax route every year, piled surplus into his operating company and never projected retirement. A defect claim reached the surplus, and at sixty he had little retirement room and a taxed exit. The root cause was a one-year horizon on a lifetime problem.

Rule 95: Never make a compensation or extraction decision on this year's tax alone; test it against a written ten-year projection, and move surplus out of any entity carrying project risk before a claim exists, on advice.

Next: Warrick, on The Money: what each savings pool really returns after tax, and the Wealth Ledger view of where money should live.
checklist: I test every compensation decision against a ten-year projection.
My accountant's engagement includes planning, not only compliance.
I have a written retirement income target.
I do not leave large surplus in an entity carrying project risk.
Any move of surplus is made on advice, before any claim exists.
I treat a lender's request for personal income as a planning signal.
I read every engagement letter for what it excludes.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite case. An owner-manager compared salary and dividend each year-end, found dividends slightly cheaper, and took only dividends for twenty years. He left surplus profit in his operating company to defer personal tax, until a hypothetical 3,000,000 dollars sat in the entity that built projects and signed guarantees. In year 19 a defect claim pursued the company and its surplus. At sixty he had little retirement room, little pension entitlement, and a taxed route out. The warning signs were a lender asking for personal income, a lawyer noting the surplus sat with the risk, and an engagement letter that said compliance only. Once the claim existed, moving the surplus would look like defeating a creditor. The root cause was a one-year horizon on a lifetime problem. Rule 95: never decide compensation or extraction on this year's tax alone; test it against a ten-year projection, and move surplus out of risk before a claim exists.
terms: Planning horizon — the length of time over which a decision's consequences are considered.
Trapped surplus — profit retained in a company that cannot be extracted without significant tax or, once a claim exists, legal risk.
Compliance engagement — an adviser engagement limited to preparing and filing returns correctly, without forward planning.

hostile.q: Your company holds 3,000,000 dollars of investments alongside its construction risk. If I'm a claimant, why can't I reach it?
hostile.a: You could today, which is why we are not leaving it there. On advice, and while no claim exists, surplus will move periodically to a holding entity for a stated business reason, with the board resolution and valuation on file. I will not try to move anything once a claim is made.

rule: Rule 95: Never make a compensation or extraction decision on this year's tax alone; test it against a written ten-year projection, and move surplus out of any entity carrying project risk before a claim exists, on advice.

title: Where a Dollar of Savings Should Live
summary: The same dollar saved in a taxable account, a tax-deferred account or a tax-free account ends twenty years later at very different after-tax values, and the ranking depends mainly on your tax rate now compared with your tax rate when you withdraw. This lesson works the comparison with illustrative rates and adds the Wealth Ledger view of after-tax net worth.
body:
A tax-deferred account beats a tax-free one when your tax rate at withdrawal is lower than your rate today, ties when they are equal, and loses when it is higher. Most of the art is in forecasting that one comparison honestly.

Recall

Q. What does a quarterly review check first, before performance?

A. The portfolio against the investment policy statement, using an independent reconciliation from the custodian's records: allocation ranges, new holdings and total cost against the ceiling.

Q. What is the equalisation gap in succession?

A. The value owed to inactive heirs, when the active heir keeps the business, minus what the rest of the estate can provide after transfer costs.

Q. What is a conflict of interest in investment advice?

A. A situation in which the adviser's own interest, such as a commission or an in-house product, could pull against the client's. Disclosure reveals it; it does not remove it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer often has more choices about where to keep money than an employee: personal accounts, tax-advantaged accounts, an operating company, a holding company. The pre-tax return can be identical in every one of them and the after-tax result very different. This lesson measures that difference. Every rate here is an illustrative assumption chosen for arithmetic; real rates, limits and rules vary by jurisdiction and change, so verify against the primary source and a licensed adviser is required before you act.

The setup

You have 10,000 dollars of pre-tax income to save for 20 years. Illustrative assumptions: your marginal tax rate today is 40 percent; the investments earn 5 percent a year before tax in every pool; in a taxable account, annual tax on income and gains reduces the effective return to 3.5 percent; and your tax rate when you withdraw is 30 percent.

A marginal tax rate is the rate on the next dollar of income, which is the rate that matters for a decision about one more dollar.

Three pools, one dollar

Taxable account. You pay 40 percent tax first, so 6,000 dollars is invested. It grows at 3.5 percent after annual tax. After 20 years: 6,000 times 1.035 to the 20th, about 1.99, is about 11,940 dollars, yours to spend.

Tax-deferred account. The contribution is deductible, so the full 10,000 dollars is invested. It grows untaxed at 5 percent. After 20 years: 10,000 times 1.05 to the 20th, about 2.65, is about 26,530 dollars. On withdrawal you pay 30 percent: you keep about 18,570 dollars.

Tax-free account. You pay 40 percent tax first, so 6,000 dollars is invested. It grows untaxed at 5 percent. After 20 years: 6,000 times 2.65 is about 15,920 dollars, and qualifying withdrawals are not taxed.

PoolInvestedAfter 20 years, after tax
Taxable6,000about 11,940
Tax-deferred, 30 percent at withdrawal10,000about 18,570
Tax-free6,000about 15,920

Say that out loud now.

The one comparison that decides it

Now change only the withdrawal rate to 40 percent, the same as today. The tax-deferred result becomes 26,530 times 0.6, about 15,920 dollars: exactly the tax-free result. That is not a coincidence. When the tax rate in equals the tax rate out, deferral and tax-free treatment produce the same answer, because each simply removes tax from the growth.

So the professional rule of thumb is this. Both sheltered pools beat the taxable account, because the growth compounds untaxed. Between the two sheltered pools, the deciding question is whether your rate at withdrawal will be lower than, equal to or higher than your rate today. A high earner expecting a modest retirement income tends to favour deferral. Someone in a low-income year, or expecting higher income later, tends to favour tax-free. Uncertainty about future rates is itself an argument for holding some of each, which is called tax diversification: spreading savings across pools with different tax treatment so you can choose, in retirement, which to draw from.

A second worked example shows why the forecast matters. A developer who expects a large sale in retirement, plus rental income, may face a withdrawal rate higher than today's. Suppose 45 percent at withdrawal. The deferred result falls to 26,530 times 0.55, about 14,590 dollars, now below the tax-free 15,920. The same account that was best for one person is second best for another, on identical returns.

The fourth pool: the company

An owner-manager can also leave profit in a company. If the corporate rate on active business income is lower than the personal rate, more money is left to invest at first, which looks attractive. But two things work against it. Investment income earned inside a company may be taxed at a different, sometimes higher, rate under special rules, and money must eventually come out, usually as a taxed dividend. Whether the company is a better or worse place than a personal pool depends entirely on the jurisdiction's rules and on how long the money stays. It also carries the risk from Day 2: money in an operating company sits beside its creditors.

The order you draw it back

Tax diversification earns its keep in decumulation. Suppose, hypothetically, a retiree needs 120,000 dollars a year and has all three pools. In a year with a large one-off taxable gain, perhaps from selling a building, the retiree can draw spending from the tax-free pool and leave the tax-deferred pool untouched, so the sale is not stacked on top of taxed withdrawals. In a quiet year with little other income, the retiree can draw more from the tax-deferred pool, filling the lower tax brackets that would otherwise go unused. The goal is a steadier taxable income across the years rather than spikes, because in a progressive system spikes are taxed at higher marginal rates.

Someone with only one pool has no such choice. That is the practical value of diversification: not a better return, but a lever in each future year. The exact sequencing depends on rules about minimum withdrawals, benefits that reduce with income, and estate treatment, all of which vary by jurisdiction.

Wealth Ledger

For your personal balance sheet, Mr Shabazz, add a column beside every asset: after-tax value. A dollar in a tax-deferred account is not a dollar of wealth; it is a dollar less the tax you will pay to withdraw it. A dollar inside a company is a dollar less the tax to extract it. A dollar in a tax-free account is close to a full dollar. Two people with the same headline net worth can have very different after-tax net worth, and only the after-tax figure tells you what you can actually spend or leave behind. Ask your accountant to estimate the column once a year with rates confirmed against the primary source.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser, on rates, limits and the treatment of each pool; licensed investment adviser, on what is held inside each.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing a savings pool on today's deduction alone, without forecasting the withdrawal rate, so deferral is used where it ends up taxed more on the way out. The control is an explicit written assumption about your future rate, revisited every year, and some tax diversification against being wrong.

The beginner's mistake

Reading the balance in a tax-deferred account as wealth. The beginner forgets that part of it belongs to the tax authority and plans spending on the gross figure.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage and Elias taught after-tax leakage: the gap between a project's pre-tax return and what the investor actually keeps. This lesson is the same idea applied to your own savings. The pool is the structure, and the structure decides the leakage, exactly as the entity did for a project.

Recap

Sheltered pools beat taxable ones because growth compounds untaxed. Between deferred and tax-free, the withdrawal rate versus today's rate decides. Hold some of each against uncertainty, treat the company as a fourth pool with its own risks, and read your net worth after tax.

Next: Elias, on The Rules: the concepts behind compensation and registered accounts, with a Canada and Guyana comparison.
checklist: I compare savings pools after tax, not before.
I write down my assumed tax rate today and at withdrawal.
I hold some savings in each pool as tax diversification.
I treat money left in a company as a fourth pool with its own risks.
My balance sheet has an after-tax value beside every asset.
I check passive income rules before investing inside a company.
A tax adviser confirms every rate and limit against the primary source.
head: Field checklist
speak: Take 10,000 dollars of pre-tax income saved for 20 years, at an illustrative 5 percent return and a 40 percent tax rate today. In a taxable account you invest 6,000, it grows at about 3.5 percent after annual tax, and you end with about 11,940. In a tax-deferred account you invest the full 10,000, it grows to about 26,530, and after an assumed 30 percent on withdrawal you keep about 18,570. In a tax-free account you invest 6,000, it grows to about 15,920, and you keep it all. If your withdrawal rate equals today's 40 percent, deferred and tax-free tie exactly. If your withdrawal rate is higher, deferral loses. So the deciding question is your rate in retirement versus now, and uncertainty argues for holding some of each. Treat money left in a company as a fourth pool with its own tax rules and creditor risk, and put an after-tax value beside every asset on your balance sheet.
terms: Marginal tax rate — the rate of tax on the next dollar of income, the rate that matters for a decision about one more dollar.
Tax diversification — spreading savings across pools with different tax treatment so withdrawals can be chosen to manage tax later.
After-tax value — what an asset is worth to you once the tax due to access or extract it is deducted.

hostile.q: You've told me your net worth includes a large retirement account. What is it worth after tax?
hostile.a: On my accountant's estimate, using an assumed withdrawal rate that I review yearly, it is worth materially less than the balance. I report it at that after-tax figure, with the rate assumption stated, so neither of us mistakes deferred tax for my equity.

title: The Rules Behind Paying Yourself and Saving
summary: The concepts that govern an owner's compensation and savings: reasonableness of salary, how dividends are taxed and integrated, rules against shifting income to family, contribution limits and withdrawal conditions on sheltered accounts, and what happens when you change country. Includes a conceptual Canada and Guyana comparison.
body:
The choices from this week sit inside rules: what a company may deduct, how a dividend is taxed, who may receive income, how much can be sheltered, and what changes if you move. Know the concepts so you know which questions to ask your adviser.

Recall

Q. In a family office, why should custody be independent of the manager?

A. So the evidence that the assets exist comes from someone other than the person managing them. That separation is what would have exposed the Madoff fraud.

Q. What gives a family constitution legal force?

A. Implementing documents, such as the shareholders' agreement, articles, trust deed and will, which carry its principles into enforceable terms.

Q. What is the risk of an in-house product recommended by an adviser?

A. The adviser's firm may earn more from it, a conflict that should be disclosed in writing with the total cost compared against outside options.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the salary-versus-dividend comparison and the choice of savings pool are only as good as the rules underneath them. Most expensive mistakes in this area are not aggressive planning; they are simple rule breaches: a contribution over the limit, a dividend paid to a family member caught by a rule against income splitting, an account that loses its tax status after a move abroad. I teach concepts only. Every rule, rate, limit and deadline must be verified against the primary source before you rely on it.

Compensation rules

Plain English. A company can usually deduct salary it pays, but tax systems often require the expense to be reasonable or incurred to earn income, so a salary paid to someone who does little work may be challenged. A dividend is not deductible, and its tax treatment for the shareholder is usually designed to reflect tax the company has already paid.

The professional framing for dividends is integration, from Day 1, and the mechanisms some systems use to achieve it. In Canada, for example, the commonly described mechanism is a gross-up of the dividend combined with a dividend tax credit, with different treatment depending on the rate of corporate tax the profit bore. The details, and whether integration is precise, must be checked against the current rules.

Applied example, hypothetical. A company pays the owner's spouse a salary for bookkeeping she does part-time. If the amount resembles what an outsider would be paid for that work, it is likely to be treated as a genuine expense. If it is far above market for minimal work, a tax authority may deny the deduction or recharacterise it. The documentation that protects it is ordinary: a job description, hours, and a comparable market rate.

Rules against shifting income

Many systems tax people at progressive rates, so there is an incentive to move income to family members with lower incomes. Many systems respond with income attribution rules: rules that tax income from property or a business on the person who transferred it or controls it, rather than on the family member who received it, in defined circumstances. Some also have specific rules aimed at dividends paid by private companies to family members who do not contribute to the business.

The concept to carry is this: paying family members through your company is possible in many systems, but the more the recipient contributes, in work or capital, the more likely the payment is to be respected. A dividend to an adult child who has no role in the business is exactly the kind of payment such rules target. Verify against the primary source before you rely on it.

Say that out loud now.

Sheltered account rules

Tax-deferred and tax-free accounts come with conditions. There are usually contribution limits, sometimes based on earned income, which is why salary matters; penalties for contributing too much; rules on what investments the account may hold; and conditions on withdrawals, such as age or purpose, with tax or penalties for breaking them. Some deferred plans must be converted to an income-paying form, with minimum withdrawals, by a certain age.

Applied example, hypothetical. An owner contributes to a tax-deferred account based on what he remembers his room to be, without checking the official statement of his limit. He over-contributes. Depending on the rules, a penalty can accrue each month until the excess is removed. The control is mechanical: confirm the official limit before every contribution.

Changing country

A sheltered account's benefits are granted by the country that created it. If you become resident elsewhere, the new country may not recognise the shelter, may tax the growth or withdrawals anyway, and may require reporting of the account as a foreign asset. Some countries also apply a departure tax concept to certain assets when a resident leaves, as Week 64 discussed. Tax-free accounts are especially vulnerable, because a foreign system may see no reason to exempt income another country chose not to tax. Treaties, from Week 57, can change the answer. Before any move, get advice from both sides.

Applied example, hypothetical. A developer with a tax-free account at home takes a long assignment abroad and becomes resident there for tax purposes. The account keeps growing and he assumes nothing has changed. His new country treats the account as an ordinary foreign investment account, taxes its annual growth, and requires it to be reported each year as a foreign asset. Two years later he learns he has two years of unreported foreign income and possible penalties for missing information returns. A one-hour meeting before the move would have let him decide whether to keep, reduce or restructure the account, and what to report.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison only. Verify against primary source before relying on any point.

Canada. Canada has a well-developed set of registered accounts, including the registered retirement savings plan, commonly described as tax-deferred, and the tax-free savings account. Integration of corporate and personal tax on dividends is a stated design feature, using a gross-up and credit mechanism. Salary generally creates earned income for retirement account room and attracts contributions to the Canada Pension Plan, while dividends generally do not. There are income attribution rules and specific rules on dividends from private companies to family members. Limits, rates and conditions change, so confirm them each year.

Guyana. Guyana levies personal income tax and corporation tax under its own statutes, and the tax treatment of dividends, salaries and approved pension arrangements follows Guyanese law [unverified — confirm independently]. Whether there are tax-advantaged savings accounts comparable to Canada's, how dividends from a Guyanese company are taxed in the hands of an individual, and how a Canadian registered account is treated by Guyana if the holder becomes resident there are all questions for a Guyanese tax adviser [unverified — confirm independently].

The practical point for anyone with ties to both: never assume a shelter granted in one country travels with you to the other.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser in each relevant country; accountant, on payroll and dividend documentation.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a simple rule breach that turns a sensible plan into a penalty: an over-contribution, a dividend caught by an attribution or family-dividend rule, or a shelter lost after a move. The control is an annual checklist confirmed by your adviser: official contribution limits, every family payment justified by contribution, and residence plans reviewed before any move.

The beginner's mistake

Paying dividends to every adult family member to use their lower tax rates, without asking whether a rule taxes that income back on the owner. The beginner sees the rate difference and misses the rule written to remove it.

Callback

In Week 24, Elias and Cole drew the line between avoidance and evasion, and taught that anti-avoidance rules look at substance over form. Paying a family member who does no work is a form without substance, which is why so many systems target it. The safe version is boring: real work, a market rate and records.

Recap

Salary must be reasonable; dividends are taxed with an eye to corporate tax already paid. Attribution and family-dividend rules limit income shifting. Sheltered accounts have limits, investment rules and withdrawal conditions. A move abroad can remove a shelter. Canada and Guyana differ, so confirm locally.

Next: Nadia, on The Numbers: a worked salary-versus-dividend comparison with illustrative rates.
checklist: Every salary my company pays is reasonable for the work done and documented.
I confirm my official contribution limits before every contribution.
Every payment to a family member is justified by real work or capital.
I check attribution and family-dividend rules before paying family members.
I know the withdrawal conditions on each sheltered account.
I get advice in both countries before changing residence.
I never assume a shelter granted in one country applies in another.
head: Field checklist
speak: Your compensation and savings choices sit inside rules, and the costly mistakes are usually simple breaches. Salary must generally be reasonable for the work done to be deductible. A dividend is not deductible, and integration aims to tax it with credit for corporate tax already paid; in Canada this is commonly described as a gross-up and dividend tax credit. Attribution rules, and specific rules on private-company dividends to family, can tax income shifted to relatives back on the owner, so payments to family should rest on real work or capital. Sheltered accounts have contribution limits, penalties for excess, investment rules and withdrawal conditions; confirm the official limit before contributing. A shelter granted by one country may not be recognised by another if you move. Canada's registered accounts are well developed; Guyana's treatment must be confirmed locally. Verify every rule against the primary source.
terms: Income attribution — rules taxing income on the person who transferred or controls property, rather than on the family member who received it, in defined cases.
Dividend tax credit — a credit some systems give shareholders for corporate tax already paid on the profit distributed, part of integration.
Contribution limit — the maximum that may be added to a sheltered account in a period, with penalties often applying to any excess.

hostile.q: Your company pays dividends to your two adult children. What do they do for the business?
hostile.a: If the answer is nothing, then before the next payment I will have my tax adviser confirm whether a rule taxes that income back on me. Any family member we pay will have a documented role or capital contribution, and the amount will reflect it.

title: Salary Versus Dividend, Worked With Illustrative Rates
summary: A step-by-step comparison of paying 100,000 dollars of company profit to an owner as salary, as a dividend, or as a mix, using rates invented for arithmetic. The one-year answer favours the dividend slightly; the lifetime answer changes once retirement room is counted.
body:
On this year's tax alone the dividend wins by a little. Count what the salary builds, retirement room and a deduction you can use, and the answer can reverse. The arithmetic shows why the decision has to be made over more than one year.

Recall

Q. What is integration in a tax system?

A. The design aim that income earned through a company and paid as a dividend bears roughly the same total tax as the same income earned directly.

Q. In the succession equalisation, why did the family test the note against the company's free cash?

A. Because the company must pay the note from free cash after debt service, and a note sized only to the arithmetic could starve the business.

Q. Why does a fee of 1 percent matter so much over twenty years?

A. Because it compounds: the cost is not only the fees paid but the growth those fees would have earned.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will have this conversation with your accountant every year. If you can do the arithmetic yourself, on round numbers, you can ask the right question: not "which is cheaper?" but "cheaper over what period, and what does each build?" Every rate below is invented for arithmetic. Real rates, contribution rates and limits vary by jurisdiction and year, so verify against the primary source, and have your tax adviser run the real figures.

The assumptions

Your company earns 100,000 dollars of profit before paying you. Illustrative rates: corporate tax on business profit, 15 percent. Employer payroll contribution on salary, 5 percent. Employee payroll contribution, 5 percent of salary. Personal tax on salary at an average rate of 30 percent. Personal tax on dividends at an effective 25 percent, lower than on salary to reflect credit for corporate tax. Retirement account room earned at 18 percent of salary. These are not any country's rates.

Option A: all salary

Step 1. Salary plus the employer contribution must equal the 100,000 dollars of profit, so the company pays no corporate tax. Salary times 1.05 equals 100,000, so salary is about 95,240 dollars and the employer contribution about 4,760.

Step 2. Employee contribution: 5 percent of 95,240, about 4,760.

Step 3. Personal tax: 30 percent of 95,240, about 28,570.

Step 4. Cash in your hand: 95,240 minus 4,760 minus 28,570, about 61,910 dollars.

Step 5. What it built: retirement room of 18 percent of 95,240, about 17,140 dollars, plus contributions toward a contributory public pension, if your jurisdiction has one.

Option B: all dividend

Step 1. Corporate tax: 15 percent of 100,000, which is 15,000 dollars. Profit after tax: 85,000.

Step 2. Pay it all as a dividend of 85,000 dollars.

Step 3. Personal tax at 25 percent: 21,250.

Step 4. Cash in your hand: 85,000 minus 21,250, which is 63,750 dollars.

Step 5. What it built: no retirement room and no pension contributions.

Say that out loud now.

The one-year answer

Option B leaves you 63,750 dollars against Option A's 61,910: about 1,840 dollars more, roughly 2 percent of the profit. That is the comparison most year-end decisions stop at, and on these assumptions it favours the dividend. Notice how close it is. When integration works reasonably well, the two routes land near each other, which is exactly why the other consequences decide the question.

The lifetime answer

Now use the retirement room Option A created. Suppose you contribute the full 17,140 dollars to a tax-deferred account. The contribution is deductible, so at your 30 percent rate it saves about 5,140 dollars of tax this year. Your after-tax cost of saving 17,140 is about 12,000 dollars.

Compare the two owners after each saves the same 12,000 dollars of after-tax money.

Owner A has 17,140 dollars working in a sheltered account, growing untaxed, taxed only on withdrawal, perhaps at a lower rate.

Owner B, with no room, puts 12,000 dollars into a taxable account, where growth is taxed every year.

From Day 3, a dollar sheltered for 20 years at 5 percent and withdrawn at a 30 percent rate keeps about 1.86 dollars after tax per dollar contributed; a dollar in a taxable account at 3.5 percent after annual tax grows to about 1.99. Owner A: 17,140 times 1.86, about 31,880 dollars after tax in twenty years. Owner B: 12,000 times 1.99, about 23,880. The salary owner is ahead by about 8,000 dollars from one year's decision, against the 1,840 dollars the dividend owner saved that year. Repeat it every year for twenty years and the gap is large.

The answer reverses if the room is never used. Salary that creates room nobody fills has paid payroll contributions for nothing. The salary only wins if the owner actually saves into the room it creates.

What changes the answer

Run three sensitivities, each on the same round numbers.

First, a worse withdrawal rate. If the salary owner expects to withdraw at 40 percent instead of 30, each sheltered dollar keeps about 1.59 dollars after tax rather than 1.86. 17,140 times 1.59 is about 27,250 dollars, still ahead of the taxable 23,880, but the lead falls from about 8,000 to about 3,400. Deferral helps less when the rate on the way out is high.

Second, retaining instead of paying out. Suppose the owner does not need the cash and leaves the 85,000 dollars of after-tax profit inside the company. Personal tax on the dividend, 21,250 dollars, is deferred, which looks attractive. But in this illustration investment income inside the company is assumed to be taxed at a higher rate than business profit, and the money still comes out as a taxed dividend later. Deferral is real; it is not exemption, and Day 2 showed what retained surplus can be exposed to.

Third, a lender's view. A bank assessing the owner for a mortgage may want to see salary on a personal return. Two years of dividend-only income can make the same owner look less qualified, even when the cash is identical. That is not tax, but it is a cost of the dividend route that belongs in the decision.

Option C: the mix

Most planners end with a mix: enough salary to create the room the owner will really use and to build pension entitlement, and the rest as dividends or retained profit. In this example, a salary sized so that 18 percent of it equals the contribution the owner can afford, with the balance as dividends. The precise point depends on real rates, limits, any cap on earnings that count for pensions, and the owner's cash needs, which is the work your adviser does with real numbers.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser or accountant, on the real rates, limits and the compensation mix.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is deciding on the one-year comparison, which is often close and slightly favours one route, while ignoring what each route builds over decades. The control is to run both the one-year and the lifetime comparison every year, with real figures from your adviser.

The beginner's mistake

Taking salary to build retirement room and then never using the room. The beginner pays the payroll cost and forgoes the benefit, which is the worst of both options.

Callback

In Week 94, Nadia reverse engineered a portfolio and found that a half point of fees was worth hundreds of thousands of dollars of required capital. This calculation has the same shape. A small annual saving looks decisive in a single year, and a slightly larger compounding benefit, repeated for twenty years, is worth far more.

Recap

With illustrative rates, the dividend left 63,750 dollars against salary's 61,910. But salary created 17,140 dollars of room, which, used for twenty years, put the salary owner about 8,000 dollars ahead from one year's choice. The answer depends on using the room; most owners land on a mix.

Next: Elias, on The Room: the year-end compensation meeting with your accountant.
checklist: I run the one-year comparison and the lifetime comparison every year.
My accountant uses real rates and limits, confirmed against the primary source.
I size any salary to the retirement room I will actually use.
I count payroll contributions on both the company and employee side.
I count pension entitlement as part of what salary builds.
I never take salary for room I leave empty.
My compensation mix is recorded by board resolution each year.
head: Field checklist
speak: Take 100,000 dollars of company profit and invented rates. As salary, the company pays about 95,240 plus a 5 percent employer contribution; after a 5 percent employee contribution and 30 percent tax, you keep about 61,910, and you have built about 17,140 dollars of retirement room. As a dividend, the company pays 15 percent tax, leaving 85,000; after 25 percent personal tax you keep 63,750, about 1,840 more, but build no room. That is where most year-end decisions stop. Now use the room. Contributing 17,140 costs about 12,000 after the deduction. Sheltered for twenty years it is worth about 31,880 after tax; the same 12,000 in a taxable account is worth about 23,880. The salary owner is ahead by about 8,000 from one year's choice. But only if the room is used. Most owners land on a mix, sized with real figures from their adviser.
terms: Payroll contributions — mandatory contributions on salary, paid by the employer, the employee or both, often toward public pensions or insurance.
Retirement room — the amount a person may contribute to a sheltered retirement account, often based on earned income.
Effective tax rate — the total tax paid divided by the income it was charged on.

hostile.q: Your own numbers show the dividend leaves you more cash this year. Why would you choose the option that costs more?
hostile.a: Because it costs about 1,840 dollars this year and, on the same assumptions, builds room worth roughly 8,000 dollars more in twenty years, as long as I use it. I will only take that salary if I commit to filling the room, and my accountant will confirm it with real rates.

title: The Year-End Meeting With Your Accountant
summary: A realistic scene: a hypothetical owner's year-end meeting with an accountant who has prepared the usual one-year salary-versus-dividend comparison. The lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent, and how to turn a compliance meeting into a planning one.
body:
The year-end meeting is where most owners hand their lifetime tax to a one-year spreadsheet. Your job is to change the question on the table from "what is cheapest this year?" to "what is best over the next ten?", without making your accountant defensive.

Recall

Q. In the Week 95 composite, what was the root cause?

A. A one-year planning horizon applied to a lifetime problem: every year's choice was optimised locally and nobody owned the sequence.

Q. In the family succession meeting, what three lists should the meeting end with?

A. What everyone agrees, what is still open, and who will do what before the next meeting.

Q. What should you ask any adviser before acting on their recommendation?

A. How they are paid, by whom, and whether the recommendation changes what they earn.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, an accountant engaged for compliance will do compliance superbly. If you want planning, you have to ask for it, scope it and pay for it. This scene is hypothetical. You are an owner-manager with a development company that earned a hypothetical 400,000 dollars of profit this year. Your accountant, whom you have used for six years, has sent a two-page comparison recommending dividends only, as in every previous year. The figures are illustrative.

Preparing the room

Before the meeting, write one page for yourself. At the top, the decision you have to make: how this year's 400,000 dollars of profit leaves the company, or stays in it. Beneath it, four facts you can supply that the accountant may not have: how much cash you personally need this year, whether you expect to borrow personally in the next two years, how much you will genuinely save, and any plan to sell, retire or move country within ten years. Each one changes the answer, and none appears on a tax return.

Then write your one required outcome: a decision made against more than one year. And your open points: the exact mix, whether surplus moves, and the fee for planning work. Bring last year's resolution, so you can see what was decided and why. You are not walking in to argue with a professional about tax law. You are walking in to give a professional the facts and the question that let them do their best work.

The scene

The accountant opens: "Same as last year. Dividends come out slightly ahead once you count payroll costs. I'd stay with that."

You say: "Thank you, that's clear. Before we decide, I'd like to look at it over ten years, not one. I'm trying to understand what each option builds, not just what it costs this year."

The accountant: "That's a bigger exercise. Our engagement is for the returns."

The question behind the question

The accountant is not refusing. The question behind "our engagement is for the returns" is "are you asking me to take on work, and responsibility, that you are not paying for?" That is a reasonable question from a professional, and it tells you the gap from Day 2 exists in your own arrangement.

And your own question has one behind it too: "Has anyone ever been responsible for my lifetime tax?" The honest answer, so far, is no.

Say that out loud now.

Lines to say

"You're right, and that's my oversight. I'd like to add a planning scope. Could you send me a proposal for a ten-year projection, updated each year before the compensation decision?"

"For this year, can you show me three options side by side: all dividend, all salary, and a salary sized to the retirement room I'll actually use, with the rest as dividends?"

"What does each option build: retirement room, pension entitlement, and income a lender will see?"

"How much surplus is sitting in the operating company, and should any of it move, on legal advice, to somewhere away from project risk?"

"Which assumptions are you least sure of?"

Lines never to say

"Just do whatever saves the most tax." That instruction produces the composite from Day 2, one correct year at a time.

"My friend pays his kids dividends, can we do that?" It invites a conversation about income attribution and family-dividend rules from the wrong end. Ask instead what the rules permit for family members who genuinely contribute.

"Why didn't you tell me this before?" It turns a gap in the engagement you signed into a fault in the person, and it will make every future answer more defensive.

"Don't put that in writing." Every compensation decision should be recorded by resolution with the reasoning, because a decision without a record is one you cannot defend later.

When to stay silent

After you ask "which assumptions are you least sure of?", stop and wait. Professionals rarely volunteer their uncertainty and often share it when asked plainly and given room. The answer usually names the assumption your plan most depends on: future tax rates, a planned sale, or whether you will actually use the room.

And when the accountant explains a rule you do not understand, do not nod. Say "Let me repeat that back to you", then repeat it. Silence that looks like understanding is how a rule breach starts.

Holding your state

Tax conversations can make a capable person feel slow: unfamiliar terms, deadlines, the sense that money is leaking somewhere you cannot see. That discomfort pushes people to decide quickly and leave. Slow down instead. Ask for the options in writing, set a date to decide before the deadline, and take the decision away to read. A compensation decision made calmly a week later is worth more than one made in the meeting.

How it ends

You leave with three things: this year's three-option comparison, a proposal for an ongoing planning engagement with a clear fee, and an action to ask your corporate lawyer about the surplus. You decide the mix the following week, record it by board resolution, and put the ten-year projection on your annual calendar for the month before every year-end.

A second scene: the adviser who over-promises

Suppose instead a new adviser tells you: "I can cut your tax by half with a structure I've used for lots of clients." The question behind that is whether you are being sold a product. Say: "Please send me the structure in writing, how it works, the rules it relies on, what could go wrong, and every fee you'd earn from it." Then show it to a second, independent adviser. Never sign anything at the first meeting, and never accept "everyone does it" as an answer; Week 24 drew the line between planning and avoidance precisely because a scheme that sounds too efficient often is.

Professional sign-off required: accountant or tax adviser, on the planning engagement and compensation mix; corporate lawyer, on moving any surplus.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a meeting that confirms last year's decision by default, because nobody has been engaged or asked to look further ahead. The control is a written planning scope with a fee, a three-option comparison every year, and a decision recorded by resolution.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the accountant's year-end recommendation as the plan. The beginner never asks what the recommendation was optimised for, or over how long.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught that the engagement letter defines what a professional is responsible for, and that silence on a point usually means it is outside scope. This scene is that lesson at your own kitchen table. "Our engagement is for the returns" is the letter speaking; the fix is to change the letter, not to blame the person.

Recap

Change the question from this year to ten years, add a planning scope, ask for three options and what each builds, ask which assumptions are weakest and wait, never instruct "whatever saves most", and record the decision by resolution.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap: six questions on the personal tax lifecycle and a Red Pen on a compensation memo.
checklist: My accountant's engagement includes a planning scope, not only compliance.
I ask for three compensation options side by side every year.
I ask what each option builds as well as what it costs.
I ask which assumptions are weakest, then wait for the answer.
I repeat back any rule I do not understand.
I decide after the meeting, not in it, and before the deadline.
Every compensation decision is recorded by board resolution.
head: Field checklist
speak: At the year-end meeting, change the question from what is cheapest this year to what is best over ten years. When your accountant recommends dividends only, as always, thank them and ask to see it over ten years. If they say the engagement is for the returns, they are right: you have not bought planning. Add a planning scope with a fee. For this year, ask for three options side by side: all dividend, all salary, and a salary sized to the retirement room you will actually use. Ask what each builds: retirement room, pension entitlement and income a lender will see. Ask about surplus sitting in the operating company. Ask which assumptions they are least sure of, and wait. Never say do whatever saves most tax, never ask them to keep it off paper, and never blame them for a gap in the engagement you signed. Decide a week later, and record it by resolution.
terms: Planning scope — the part of an adviser's engagement covering forward-looking advice, as distinct from preparing returns.
Board resolution — a formal written decision of a company's directors, used to record decisions such as compensation.
Three-option comparison — a side-by-side analysis of all-dividend, all-salary and mixed compensation, with what each costs and builds.

hostile.q: I'm your accountant. Dividends have been right for six years. Are you saying I've been giving you bad advice?
hostile.a: No. You've done exactly what I engaged you to do, and done it well. I hadn't asked anyone to look beyond the year, which is my gap, not yours. I'd like to add that to your scope and pay for it.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 95 Review: Paying Yourself, Sheltering Savings, Drawing Income
summary: Six questions on the personal tax lifecycle with answers, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a hypothetical year-end compensation memo, and a two-minute boardroom drill explaining how an owner-manager plans tax over a lifetime.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: decide how money leaves your company, where you save it and how you draw it back against a ten-year projection, because a lifetime of cheapest-this-year choices is rarely the cheapest lifetime.

Recall

Q. When do a tax-deferred and a tax-free account produce the same after-tax result?

A. When the tax rate on withdrawal equals the tax rate when the money was contributed, because each then removes tax from the growth alone.

Q. What is Rule 93?

A. Never pass a company to more than one heir without a signed shareholders' agreement, made in your lifetime, that names who decides, how a deadlock breaks and how an exit is priced.

Q. What is the difference between a fee charged as a percentage of assets and a flat fee as a portfolio grows?

A. A percentage fee rises automatically with the portfolio whether or not the work does; a flat fee stays the same, so the relationship should be re-priced every few years.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you can answer these six questions aloud without notes, you can run your own year-end meeting and steer it toward the lifetime view. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What are the three phases of the personal tax lifecycle, and the tax question in each?

Answer: Accumulation: how to extract and save money efficiently. Transition: how to realise value, such as a sale, without unnecessary tax. Decumulation: in what order to draw from different pools to keep lifetime tax low and income steady.

Question 2. What is integration, and why does it make salary versus dividend a close call?

Answer: The design aim, in some systems, that income paid through a company as a dividend bears about the same total tax as income earned directly. Where it works well, the one-year tax difference is small, so other consequences decide.

Question 3. What can salary build that a dividend usually does not?

Answer: In many systems, earned income that creates retirement account room, entitlement to contributory public pensions, and personal income a lender can see. Confirm against the rules where you live.

Question 4. Between a tax-deferred and a tax-free account, what decides which is better?

Answer: Your tax rate at withdrawal compared with your rate when contributing. Lower later favours deferral; equal ties; higher favours tax-free. Uncertainty argues for holding some of each.

Question 5. Why is money left in an operating company risky as well as tax-deferred?

Answer: It sits beside the company's creditors and project claims, may face special rules on passive income, and must eventually come out as taxed income. Once a claim exists, moving it can look like defeating a creditor.

Question 6. What simple rule breaches turn a sensible plan into a penalty?

Answer: Over-contributing to a sheltered account, paying family members in ways attribution or family-dividend rules tax back on the owner, an unreasonable salary deduction, and assuming a shelter survives a move abroad.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Elias set out the lifecycle, salary versus dividend, integration and the savings pools. Ford and Cole took a composite owner who chose the cheapest route every year for twenty years, giving Rule 95. Warrick compared taxable, tax-deferred and tax-free pools and added after-tax net worth to the Wealth Ledger. Elias set out the rules on compensation, attribution, sheltered accounts and moving country, with a Canada and Guyana comparison. Nadia worked salary against dividend and showed the lifetime answer can reverse the one-year one. Elias ran the year-end meeting with an accountant.

The Red Pen

Here is a hypothetical year-end compensation memo. Find the defects before reading on.

Memo to file. Year-end compensation. Recommendation: pay the owner all dividends again this year as it is cheapest. Also pay equal dividends to the owner's two adult children to use their lower tax rates. Leave the remaining 900,000 dollars of surplus in the operating company to defer tax. The owner will top up his retirement account to last year's amount. No resolution needed as the owner is the sole director. Based on rates from two years ago.

The defects. First, "cheapest" is a one-year test with no projection of what the dividend route forgoes, the pattern behind Rule 95. Second, dividends to adult children with no stated role invite attribution or family-dividend rules that may tax the income back on the owner; the memo names no contribution by them. Third, leaving 900,000 dollars in the operating company keeps it exposed to project claims and possibly to passive income rules, and says nothing about moving it on advice while no claim exists. Fourth, an all-dividend year creates no new retirement room, so "topping up to last year's amount" may over-contribute and trigger a penalty; the limit must be confirmed against the official figure. Fifth, a sole director still needs a written resolution, because the record is what makes the decision defensible. Sixth, rates from two years ago are stale; every rate and limit must be verified against the current primary source.

The corrected memo would show three options with a ten-year projection, justify any family payment by real work or capital, address the surplus with legal advice, confirm the official contribution limit, attach a resolution, and cite current rates.

Kema's note on reading any tax memo: look for the word that hides a time period. "Cheapest", "defer" and "top up" all sound complete and all depend on when. Cheapest this year, deferred until when, topped up against which year's room? A memo that cannot answer "over what period?" for each of its recommendations has not yet done the planning.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a fellow business owner who asks, "Should I pay myself salary or dividends?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "On this year's tax alone, it's often close, because many systems try to tax both routes about the same. So the real question is what each builds. Salary usually creates retirement room, pension entitlement and income a bank can see. Dividends avoid payroll costs and are flexible, but build none of that. I decide against a ten-year projection, not the year-end spreadsheet, and I size any salary to the room I'll actually use. I keep surplus out of the company that carries project risk, I only pay family members who genuinely work in the business, and I compare savings pools after tax. Then I record the decision by resolution and have my adviser confirm the current rules."

Score yourself. Did you say it depends on what each builds? Did you mention the ten-year view? Did you mention surplus and family payments? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is optimising one year at a time, so the lifetime cost arrives at retirement when it cannot be fixed. The control is a ten-year projection, owned under a planning engagement, reviewed before every year-end decision.

The beginner's mistake

Reading a sheltered account balance, or company surplus, as spendable wealth. Both carry tax still to pay on the way out, and only the after-tax figure is yours.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught the decision journal: write down what you decided, why, and what you expected, so you can learn from the result. A year-end compensation resolution with its reasoning is a decision journal for your tax. Read twenty of them in a row and you would have seen the composite owner's mistake by year five.

Recap

Plan the lifecycle over ten years. Salary and dividend are close on tax and differ in what they build. Choose savings pools by comparing tax rates now and later. Keep surplus away from project risk, pay family on substance, and confirm every rule. Rule 95 keeps the horizon long.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on First Principles: post-mortem three, the cross-border and personal wealth failures that recur.
checklist: What are the three phases of the personal tax lifecycle, and the tax question in each?
What is integration, and why does it make salary versus dividend a close call?
What can salary build that a dividend usually does not?
Between a tax-deferred and a tax-free account, what decides which is better?
Why is money left in an operating company risky as well as tax-deferred?
What simple rule breaches turn a sensible plan into a penalty?
head: The six questions
speak: This week's core: lifetime tax depends on three recurring choices, how money leaves your company, where you save it, and the order you draw it back. In many systems integration makes salary and dividend close on one year's tax, so decide on what each builds: salary usually creates retirement room, pension entitlement and income a lender sees. Between tax-deferred and tax-free accounts, the deciding question is your tax rate at withdrawal against your rate now; hold some of each. Money left in an operating company is deferred, not free, and sits beside its creditors. Simple breaches cause most penalties: over-contributing, paying family members without substance, an unreasonable salary, assuming a shelter survives a move. Rule 95: never decide compensation or extraction on this year's tax alone; test it against a written ten-year projection, and move surplus out of project risk before a claim exists, on advice.
terms: Ten-year projection — a forward model of income, tax and account balances used to test each year's compensation and savings decisions.
Extraction — taking value out of a company, by salary, dividend, loan repayment or other routes, each with its own tax treatment.
Lifecycle tax planning — planning tax across accumulation, transition and decumulation rather than one year at a time.

hostile.q: You've chosen salary this year even though dividends were cheaper. Isn't that just paying more tax?
hostile.a: It costs a little more this year. It also builds retirement room I will fill and pension entitlement, which on a ten-year projection is worth more than the saving. I'll show you the projection and the resolution recording the decision.
